_readme: Ready-to-apply permission allowlist. Reduces prompts for SAFE operations only.
HOW TO APPLY (per machine — settings files are gitignored and do NOT propagate):
Merge the permissions.allow array below into ~/.claude/settings.json
(all projects on that machine) or into a project .claude/settings.local.json.
Append to the existing allow array; do not replace it.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE — leave these in your `ask` list, they are the
gates that stop an agent taking production down:
git push / git reset --hard / rm -rf
gh pr create|merge|ready, gh api POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE
supabase db push, mcp Supabase apply_migration|execute_sql|merge_branch|delete_branch
vercel promote / vercel rollback, prisma migrate deploy
Generated 19/08/2026 from the operations that actually caused prompts in a long
autonomous session. Read-only inspection, local-only git, the build/test loop,
and sibling reviewer CLIs.
THE CLAIM THIS FILE USED TO MAKE, AND WHY IT WAS WITHDRAWN (20/08/2026).
The line above previously ended '- nothing that mutates production or pushes
code.' That was not true and could not be made true. Two independent review
rounds removed a blanket psql grant and blanket scripts/ grants for exactly that
reason, and a third pointed out the entries that make the claim unachievable in
principle: Bash(node:*), Bash(python3:*), Bash(python:*) and Bash(npx:*) are
GENERAL-PURPOSE INTERPRETERS. `node -e` can open a database client, spawn a
command this list denies, or make an arbitrary network call. No prefix-matching
allowlist can permit an interpreter and still guarantee anything about what it
does.
They are KEPT, because removing them makes the file useless for the loop it
exists to serve, and the CLAIM is corrected instead. A safety artefact that
overstates its guarantee is worse than one with a narrower honest scope, because
it is read as assurance. What this file actually provides:
* it reduces prompts for operations that were observed to be routine and safe;
* it deliberately withholds the named production/push commands in the list above,
so those still prompt by NAME;
* it does NOT and cannot prevent a granted interpreter from reaching production
by another route. That boundary is enforced by the pr-release-gate hook and by
review, not by this file.
REMOVED 19/08/2026: Bash(psql:*). An independent review (openrouter) found it
contradicted the line above: the permission language matches a command PREFIX and
cannot see the connection URI, so a blanket psql grant authorises arbitrary DDL and
DML against ANY database the machine can reach — including the production project
this very branch exists to stop an agent mutating. The ship-gates will now prompt
for psql, which is the correct default. Re-add only as a narrower rule that cannot
reach production, and never as psql:*.
REMOVED 20/08/2026, same round, same class: Bash(scripts/:*), Bash(./scripts/:*)
and Bash(bash scripts/:*). A blanket grant over a DIRECTORY authorises every
executable in it with arbitrary arguments - and this repo's ship-gate scripts
take an admin connection URI and issue CREATE DATABASE, DROP DATABASE and DDL.
Pointing one at a production URI therefore mutated production with no prompt, by
a path that never mentions psql. Removing the psql rule alone did not restore the
boundary this file claims. Grant individual scripts that cannot reach production,
never a directory.
